analysis.one_liner: Speeds up generic drug competition by limiting brand-name patent-delay tactics.
analysis.headline: The bill to speed up generic drug approvals was referred to the Senate health committee in July 2002 and died there with no vote and no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it harder for brand-name drug companies to use patent tricks to keep cheaper generic versions off the market. It limited the automatic 30-month delay that a brand-name company can trigger against a generic applicant, and it stripped the 180-day head start awarded to the first generic applicant if that company stalls — including by settling with the brand-name maker instead of selling the drug. It also targeted prescription-only drugs that are sold as if they were still prescription-only. The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee and never moved again before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take brand-name prescription drugs, and the insurers and employers who pay for them, would benefit if generics reached the market sooner. When a generic copy of a drug launches, its price typically falls sharply compared with the brand-name original.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and employers buying brand-name drugs

how_it_helps.text: The bill limited the 30-month delay of generic approval: it restricted that automatic stay to patents that were already listed before the generic application was filed, and barred a brand-name company from later suing over a patent it failed to sue on within 45 days of notice [S3].

It forced the first generic applicant to give up its 180-day exclusive marketing window — which passes to no one, delaying all generic competition — if the company fails to launch within 30 days of approval, withdraws, switches its legal filing, stalls past deadlines, or signs a settlement with the brand-name maker that the Federal Trade Commission finds violates antitrust law [S3].

It deemed a drug misbranded — subject to seizure — if it was sold as prescription-only after the FDA had approved it for over-the-counter sale, closing a way brand companies keep selling at prescription prices [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies, which would lose years of extended exclusive sales and could no longer pay generic makers to stay off the market through anticompetitive settlements.

drawbacks.text: Stripping the 180-day exclusivity from a first generic filer who delays transfers that window to no one — a subsequent filer gets no exclusivity at all — which could discourage the expensive first challenges to weak brand patents in some cases [S3].

Tightening the 45-day window for patent suits and limiting the 30-month stay could push more patent disputes into court faster, raising litigation costs for both brand and generic makers, costs that could be passed through to prices [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — earlier generic competition on high-priced brand-name drugs, which reliably brings large price drops — outweighs the costs, which fall mostly on the brand-name industry's extended patent revenue. The exclusivity-forfeiture design is imperfect and could deter some first-filer challenges, but it targets a real loophole where a generic firm locks up its head start and then never launches.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate health committee in July 2002 and never got a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Sen. Judd Gregg introduced the bill on July 29, 2002 [S1, S5].
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day, and the record shows no further action [S5].
The 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, so the bill died in committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers kept the patent-delay tools and settlement practices the bill targeted, and consumers kept paying brand-name prices longer. Nothing changed for patients because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers kept the status quo

for.name: Sen. Judd Gregg
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Hampshire; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 29, 2002 to restrict patent-delay tactics against generic drugs [S1, S5].

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Edward Kennedy (D-MA) in the 107th Congress
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no markup, hearing, or vote was ever scheduled [S5].

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Industry whose extended patent monopolies and generic-settlement practices the bill restricted
against.what_they_did: The record shows no cosponsors joined and the committee never acted; the bill's targets — 30-month stays and anticompetitive settlements — were core industry practices.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no senator cosponsored the bill, so there is no record of partisan support or opposition beyond the Republican sponsor.

industries.note: The bill would cut off the automatic 30-month approval delay for later-listed patents, forfeit the first generic filer's 180-day exclusivity in delay scenarios including anticompetitive settlements, and expose prescription-only marketing of over-the-counter-approved drugs to misbranding penalties. Each provision shortens the period of brand-only sales at brand prices. The industry's interest in keeping these tools runs directly against patients seeking cheaper generics.

The bill speeds generic entry by limiting 30-month stays and letting subsequent applications proceed when the first filer forfeits exclusivity. But it also takes the valuable 180-day head start away from the first filer in more situations and gives it to no one, which shrinks the reward for challenging weak patents.
